Pakistan-based AI startup Metal has raised $4.5 million in a seed funding round led by a16z speedrun and Y Combinator.
Founded by former Airlift Technologies CEO Usman Gul, Metal serves as an AI operating system that provides deep intelligence and automation to streamline fundraising and venture capital workflows for startup founders.
The round also saw backing from Pioneer Fund, Rebel Fund, Gaingels, Indus Valley Capital, Team Ignite Ventures, and Phaze Ventures, following an earlier strategic investment by Rebel Fund in June.
Metal has posted six consecutive quarters of 30–80% quarter-on-quarter growth and is tracking to close FY2026 with multi-million-dollar annual revenue. Alongside the raise, the company has released its thesis on the future evolution of private capital markets.

Usman Gul built his second startup around a problem he spent years living through at his first. Metal, the AI company he founded in 2024, has raised $4.5 million in seed funding led by a16z Speedrun and Y Combinator, developing software that helps founders find suitable investors and manage the fundraising process.

The product grew directly out of Gul's time at Airlift, the quick commerce startup that raised $85 million in 2021 and shut down a year later when it couldn't secure another round. He says the team spoke to around 300 investors while raising roughly $120 million, with about 80% ultimately not fitting the company's stage, sector, or geography. Metal now says its paying customers have raised $542 million through the platform this year, with more than 1,000 founders using it annually and six consecutive quarters of 30% to 80% growth.

Yesterday, Sam Altman and the OpenAI for Startups team joined 200+ founders from the a16z speedrun 007 batch for a private Ask Me Anything (AMA) in SF.

The questions were the signal:
• What durable moats remain?
• What are founders still underestimating about AI?
• Will superintelligence come from one giant model or many specialized, collaborating models?
• How do humans stay meaningfully involved as machines become more capable?
• Where are the real opportunities in AI infrastructure over the next five years?

One of my favorite "hard truth" moments from the AMA was when Sam said “Every time a new technology comes along, startup founders think they get a pass on the physics of business because they’re doing the new thing.” 

My takeaway: AI does not repeal solid business fundamentals. Speed is becoming table stakes. Judgment, distribution, trust, and learning rate are where durable companies will be built. 

Special shout out to Macy Mills, David George and the entire a16z speedrun team for bringing the founder community together for this conversation!

My top-3 takeaways from QA with Sam Altman yesterday at a16z speedrun:
1. Enterprise-hacking agents are here.
2. AI diffusion is still slow.
3. Tokenmaxxing is over.

First, the Hugging Face incident shows what's possible: hundreds of persistent, unhinged frontier agents can probably hack an average enterprise. Yes, alignment problems are now a reality for everyone, and I think we'll see similar hacks in the enterprise in the near future.

Second, despite Astra-level models being around the corner, the AI diffusion is still slow. I see that with the companies I talk to: lots of token spent with limited P&L impact. However, it seems like next gen models will start connecting some of the missing dots for autonomous agents (assuming alignment will get better!).

Third, it's hard to find people more pro-tokenmaxxing than OAI folks, Peter Openclaw and me, but this Wild West era is ending. It's great to see that both Astra and Fable 5.1 are more token-efficient. I think both things will happen soon: frontier models will get cheaper as new compute ramps up and token-efficiency will keep improving. Both are great for humanity!

Y Combinator said no to my startup today.

​I’m not gonna pretend it didn't hurt it really sucked opening that email. When you’re building as a solo founder, there’s no co-founder to share the weight with. Every late night, every line of code, and every application mistake falls 100% on you.

​I applied to Y Combinator with a vision to solve a massive problem: AI tools having direct, unmonitored access to our private databases, passwords, and sensitive data.

​Right now, developers rely on complex frameworks or heavy enterprise tools like LangChain, LlamaIndex, or Snyk to manage data and security. 

But I wasn't trying to build just another complex tool for hardcore security engineers. I was building something radically better and simpler... a seamless AI permission layer that anyone can use without needing a security degree.

​I still believe in this vision, but reading my application again... Garry Tan  and the YC team made the right call. The execution just wasn't ready. The messaging was messy, and I let my excitement blind me to the flaws in my current setup. Rejection is a harsh mirror, but it's the only one that tells you the truth.

​Seeing that over 50% of accepted YC startups are repeat applicants saved my mood. This isn't a dead end it just means I have to build a product so good it can't be ignored.

​So no more sulking. Time to go back to the code, talk to real users, and make AI data control dead-simple for everyone.

​Insha'Allah, I'll be back for the next batc

🚨 One of the most creative counter drone solutions I have seen just raised $7M and it fits in a backpack. 🚨 

mara closed a pre-seed round led by Khosla Ventures with participation from a16z speedrun, Night Capital, Protagonist, Freedom Fund VC, and Indicator Fund. The San Francisco based startup is building Spike, an autonomous counter drone system designed specifically to stop the FPV drone threat that is reshaping battlefields worldwide.

Here is what makes Spike different. It has two modular components working together. Spotter is the targeting unit, combining visual, acoustic, and optional radar sensors with onboard AI for day, night, and all weather detection. Seeker is the interceptor, a 250 gram, tube launched drone flying at 200 kmph with onboard intelligence to find and intercept its target. A single launcher holds up to 48 Seekers and reloads in under a minute.

The cost advantage is the real story. A complete Spike system runs between $30,000 and $100,000. It can engage dozens of drone threats simultaneously. That is a 20x cost advantage over most existing interceptors, priced at parity with the attack drones it is built to stop.

Ground mounted systems deploy by end of 2026. Vehicle mounted and man portable versions follow in 2027.

The FPV drone problem is not going away. Mara is building the most scalable answer to it yet.

Philipp Baumanns had already signed his full-time contract at McKinsey.

Then he walked away.

The problem wasn’t that McKinsey looked bad.

It looked too good.

Good salary. Great benefits. Job security.

And that was exactly the problem.

Philipp’s thinking was simple: the longer he stayed, the harder it would become to leave.

So he joined Enpal instead.

He was employee #2 in the heat pump unit. A year later, the team had grown to more than 150 people.

Then he left again.

This time with no salary, no customers and no certainty that any of their ideas would work.

Their first idea failed.

Their first Y Combinator application got rejected.

With the next idea, they landed their first paying customers within two weeks.
That idea became telli.

Today, telli has more than 30 people, went through Y Combinator and recently announced a 15M Seed round.

In Episode 4 of GABWAF, Philipp talks about why comfortable careers become harder and harder to leave, what he learned building at Enpal, and what changed once they got to YC.

Full episode is out now. Link in the comments.

Slack started as a failed video game.
Instagram was a cluttered check-in app nobody wanted.
Shopify was just a guy trying to sell snowboards online.

None of them became what they were supposed to be.
And that’s exactly why they won.

Stewart Butterfield killed his game and turned the internal chat tool into Slack.
Kevin Systrom stripped Burbn down to photos and filters that became Instagram.
Tobias Lütke realized the software behind his snowboard store was the real product. That became Shopify.

A more recent one:
In 2025, two 22- and 23-year-old founders joined YC planning to build AI agents for finance.

Meanwhile the ones who couldn’t let go:

Kodak invented the digital camera and buried it to protect film.
Blockbuster was offered Netflix for $50 million and said no.
BlackBerry kept defending the physical keyboard while the market moved on.

Here’s the difference:

Winners treat their original idea like a hypothesis.
Losers treat it like their identity.

Pivot isn’t failure.

It’s the only move that actually wins.
You either listen to the market…

or you die arguing with it.
Which one are you?

Here are 5 design decisions behind LinkedIn’s AI code review system — 79,000+ weekly reviews, 7,500+ repos, 63.9% developer acceptance rate:

1. Multi-agent consensus, not a single model
Multiple specialized agents review the same PR independently. Only findings that overlap across agents get flagged as high-confidence. No single model is trusted alone — consensus is the reliability mechanism.

2. A 3-tier context hierarchy
Org-wide policies → repo-level standards → case-specific guidance. The system encodes what each codebase’s team actually cares about, layer by layer. No general model has this knowledge without it being explicitly provided.

3. Acceptance rates vary sharply by category
Concurrency bugs: 100%. Logic errors: 80%. Security issues: 40.6%. AI reviewers are most effective exactly where human attention drifts most — concurrency being the clearest example, where reasoning about parallel execution under time pressure is genuinely hard.

4. Two-sided evaluation
Pre-merge: blind pairwise LLM comparison to catch regressions before they ship. Post-merge: tracking 5,230 developer-accepted comments from real merged PRs as ground truth. One measurement layer without the other leaves you flying blind.

5. Infrastructure as a first-class concern
12 concurrent reviews per Kubernetes worker, ~90s from PR open to first review, 99.1% task completion rate. These are production SLOs, not aspirational targets.

A digital fashion house in Vogue. 
A developer framework backed by Y Combinator. 
A regtech platform for the most regulated market in the world.

The city is building the product, but the business goes elsewhere.

When you look at open positions, 16 open roles in Zagreb, mostly technical and operational. Commercial roles are being hired outside Croatia entirely.

This is one of the biggest blockers for regional ecosystem growth. 

The technical talent stays. The commercial function is being built where the customers are, hired locally in London, Berlin, or New York. And when revenue is built outside, so is the network, the knowledge, and eventually the next company.

If the plan is to grow the ecosystem, solving the commercial layer locally has to be part of it.

There's a cyclical theme in what startups are adopting as gtm/growth and marketing strategies.

Palantir Technologies coined the term "forward deployed engineer" in the early 2000s as a military reference to sending troops 'close to the battlefield'. 

FDE - a software engineer who embeds directly within a customer’s organization or physical workspace to build, customize, and deploy technical solutions.

Today we're seeing this wave in marketing. Just in the last 2 days I've seen atleast 4-5 startup founders/growth folks acquiring customers in this "forward-deployed" motion.

Meta Ads, Email Marketing, Content was probably the easiest and most affordable way to start distribution in the last decade - but now it is also the least impressionable of all, and the most crowded channel.

It's not at all dead - but it's just become an increasingly complex channel to crack distribution. Startups now have to over-deliver before they even pitch: free audits, custom demos, 30-60-90 plans showing exactly how the product changes your life. 

All before "want to buy this?"

First it was billboards, expo booths, door-knocking. Then it was finding your way onto someone's phone. Now growth hacks look like billboards and door-knocking again — just repackaged for people who've been trained to ignore ads.

PSA: New case study unlocked 🔓

OpenTag (YC S26) is building an AI coworker that lives inside Slack and Microsoft Teams and handles operational work from end to end.

As a core part of their enrichment infrastructure, Open Tag needed to research people and companies in real time, roles, backgrounds, teams, profiles, and sources.

Instead of building and maintaining its own crawling and parsing infrastructure, the team gave its agent our integration prompt.

Two minutes later, it had integrated Context.dev (YC S26) itself.

Now, a user can ask about someone directly in Slack, Context.dev (YC S26) fetches and structures the live web data, and OpenTag returns a sourced answer in the same thread.

No separate research workflow. No raw crawl output. No crawling infrastructure to maintain.
Just live web context, exactly when the agent needs it.
